text: Paraceratherium was a giant relative of the rhinoceros that lived in Asia between about 34 and 23 million years ago. It had no horn. Instead, it had long legs, a long neck and a head held so high it could browse leaves from the tops of trees, like a giraffe.

It stood up to about 4.8 m at the shoulder, higher than a double-decker bus, and weighed perhaps 11 to 20 tonnes, as much as three or four elephants. Its [[fossil|fossils]] have been found in Pakistan, China, Mongolia and Kazakhstan. It is one of the biggest land [[mammal|mammals]] ever known.

st.reveal: Paraceratherium belonged to the rhino family tree, though it had no horn and much longer legs and neck. It reached high branches the way a giraffe does today.

sec.t:
Today's rhinos, like the one-horned rhinos of [[@rhino-kaziranga|Kaziranga]], are heavy, low and horned. Paraceratherium belonged to a branch of the rhino family that went a different way. Its legs were long and pillar-like, and its feet had three toes, as rhino feet still do.

Its skull was about 1.3 m long, yet quite small for its huge body. Scientists think it had a flexible upper lip, perhaps a short trunk-like snout, for stripping leaves. Two big, tusk-like front teeth pointed downwards, probably for snapping branches.

When Paraceratherium lived, the dinosaurs had been gone for more than 30 million years, and [[@mammals-rise|mammals]] had grown big. Much of Asia was open woodland with scattered trees. A tall browser had the high leaves to itself, the same trick the [[@power-giraffe-neck|giraffe]] uses today.

An animal this size would have needed hundreds of kilograms of leaves every day. Its sheer bulk protected adults from almost every [[predator|predator]]. Babies were probably at risk from big crocodiles and other hunters. Like elephants today, a mother may have carried her calf for well over a year before it was born, and guarded it closely.

Its feet were probably wider than dinner plates, and each step of an adult must have landed with a heavy thud.

In 2021, Chinese scientists described a new [[species|species]] from Gansu in north-west China. They suggested these giants moved between Mongolia and South Asia, possibly through lowlands where the Tibetan Plateau now stands. At that time, the [[@himalaya-form|Himalaya]] and Tibet were still rising, as India pushed slowly into Asia.

Why did Paraceratherium die out? The [[climate|climate]] was cooling and drying, forests shrank, and big animals need big supplies of food. Other plant-eaters, including early elephants spreading from Africa, may also have competed with it for trees.

sec.h: Bigger than a rhino, smaller than a dinosaur
sec.t:
Paraceratherium is often called the largest land mammal ever. That title is now in doubt. Some scientists estimate that an [[extinct|extinct]] straight-tusked elephant whose fossils were found in India's Narmada valley may have been heavier still, though its remains are few.

Either way, the giants of the dinosaur age were in another league. [[@argentinosaurus|Argentinosaurus]], a long-necked sauropod from South America, may have weighed 70 tonnes or more, about as much as four Paraceratheriums put together.

text: Jantar Mantar is the name of five [[observatory|observatories]] built in the early 1700s by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II, the ruler who founded [[@rajasthan-forts|Jaipur]]. Instead of telescopes, they are filled with giant instruments made of stone, brick and plaster, used to track the Sun, Moon and stars with the naked eye.

The largest and best preserved is in [[@jaipur|Jaipur]]. It has about 20 main instruments, including the Samrat Yantra, a sundial about 27 m tall. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 2010. There is another famous Jantar Mantar in [[@delhi|Delhi]], and smaller ones in Ujjain and [[@varanasi|Varanasi]]. The fifth, in Mathura, has disappeared.
The name comes from "yantra", meaning instrument, and "mantra", which can mean formula or calculation.

st.prompt: The Samrat Yantra in Jaipur is a sundial. Why did Jai Singh make it so enormous?

options.t: A bigger sundial spreads the shadow out, so time can be read more exactly
So people could see it from other cities

st.reveal: On a small sundial, the shadow moves only a tiny distance each minute. Make the dial huge, and the same minute is spread over several centimetres. The Jaipur dial's shadow moves about 1 mm a second, so careful readers can tell the time to within a few seconds.

sec.h: A king who loved the sky
sec.t:
Jai Singh II became ruler of Amber, near today's Jaipur, in 1699, when he was a boy. He grew up studying mathematics and astronomy. He found that the star tables used in his time often gave wrong positions for the planets and the times of [[@eclipses|eclipses]].

Metal instruments were small and could bend or wear. So Jai Singh decided to build huge ones in stone, which he thought would be steadier and more accurate. He collected books on astronomy in [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]], Persian and Arabic, and sent scholars to learn about methods used in other countries. The result was a set of tables of star and planet positions, dedicated to the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah.

Other instruments are just as unusual. The Jai Prakash Yantra is a pair of bowls sunk into the ground, each one a map of the sky turned inside out. A cross-wire above them casts a small shadow onto the marked surface, showing where the Sun is in the sky.

The Ram Yantra is a pair of round, roofless buildings with pillars and marked floors, used to measure how high a star or planet is and in which direction. The Rashivalaya Yantra is a group of 12 instruments, one for each sign of the [[zodiac|zodiac]]. [[astronomer|Astronomers]] and astrologers of the time used it to measure the positions of the [[@constellations|constellations]] along the Sun's path.

After Jai Singh died in 1743, astronomy based on telescopes took over, and naked-eye observatories fell out of use. Some instruments crumbled. In the early 1900s, the Jaipur instruments were restored, and they still work today.

For visitors, the Jaipur observatory is a playground of strange shapes. With a guide, students can see how people measured the sky without any electronics. The Delhi Jantar Mantar, close to Connaught Place, is also well known as a place where people gather for peaceful protests.

Ancient Indian astronomers had calculated the sky with [[@astronomy-ancient-india|mathematics and careful observation]] for over a thousand years. Jai Singh's stone instruments were one of the last great efforts of that tradition before the telescope changed everything.

text: Space junk, or space debris, is anything made by people that is circling Earth but no longer does a useful job. It includes dead satellites, empty rocket stages, tools dropped by astronauts, and millions of bits from explosions and collisions, right down to flecks of paint.

The European Space Agency tracks about 40,000 objects, and estimates there are more than 50,000 pieces larger than 10 cm, about the size of an orange. There are about a million between 1 cm and 10 cm, and well over 100 million smaller than that. Because they travel so fast, even small pieces can damage working [[@satellites-help|satellites]] and the [[@space-station|International Space Station]].

st.prompt: How fast does a typical piece of space junk travel in low orbit?
st.reveal: Anything orbiting a few hundred kilometres up has to move at about 28,000 km/h, roughly ten times faster than a rifle bullet, or it would fall. At that speed, even a tiny fleck carries enough energy to crack a window or puncture a thin wall.

Most debris burns up as it falls through the air, and what survives usually lands in the ocean. Only one person is known to have been touched by space debris, Lottie Williams in Oklahoma in 1997, and she was not hurt.

sec.t:
To stay in [[orbit|orbit]] a few hundred kilometres up, an object has to move at about 28,000 km/h. Two objects on crossing paths can hit each other at even higher speeds.

At that speed, a piece the size of a marble can wreck a satellite. Even a speck of paint can pit a window. In 2016, the British astronaut Tim Peake photographed a chip about 7 mm across in one of the space station's windows. It was probably made by a fleck of paint or metal only a few thousandths of a millimetre wide.

The space station has shields to stop small bits. For bigger ones, ground controllers track the debris and, when something will pass too close, fire the station's engines to nudge it out of the way. This happens a few times a year.

The first satellite, [[@sputnik|Sputnik]], went up in 1957. Since then, thousands of [[@rockets-how|rockets]] have left upper stages, covers and bolts in orbit. Old batteries and fuel tanks have sometimes exploded, scattering pieces.

In February 2009, an American communications satellite called Iridium 33 crashed into Kosmos-2251, a dead Russian satellite, about 790 km above Siberia. It was the first accidental crash between two whole satellites, and it created thousands of new pieces. Tests in which countries destroyed their own satellites with missiles have added more.

Today, companies are launching thousands of small satellites to provide internet from space, so orbits are getting busier than ever.

Low down, a few hundred kilometres up, there are still faint traces of air. They slowly drag on debris until it falls and burns up, usually within a few years or decades. Higher up, junk can stay in orbit for centuries.

When big objects do come down, most of them burn up. In 1979, the 77-tonne US space station Skylab came down over the Indian Ocean and Western Australia. The local council of Esperance sent NASA a 400-dollar fine for littering. It went unpaid for 30 years, until an American radio host raised the money.

Space agencies now ask satellite operators to bring their spacecraft down within a set number of years after their missions end, or move them to out-of-the-way "graveyard" orbits. Some new satellites carry extra fuel just for this.

Engineers are also testing ways to grab old junk, with robotic arms, nets and magnets. In 2024, a Japanese spacecraft flew close to an old rocket stage and photographed it, a first step towards catching it. Keeping orbits clean matters for everyone who uses [[@weather-forecasts|weather forecasts]], satellite TV or [[@gps-how|GPS]].

text: समुद्र में धूप तेज़ी से फीकी पड़ती है। लगभग 1,000 मीटर से नीचे धूप बिल्कुल नहीं पहुँचती, जैसा तुम [[@ocean-zones|समुद्र की परतों]] में देख सकते हो। इसलिए बहुत-से जीव अपनी रोशनी खुद बनाते हैं। इस तरकीब को [[@bioluminescence|बायोल्यूमिनेसेंस]] कहते हैं। वे ल्यूसिफ़ेरिन नाम के एक रसायन को ऑक्सीजन और एक मददगार [[molecule|अणु]] के साथ मिलाते हैं, और इस मेल से ठंडी चमक निकलती है।

यह कितना आम है? कैलिफ़ोर्निया के पास हुए एक अध्ययन में वैज्ञानिकों ने रोबोट [[@submarines|पनडुब्बियों]] से फ़िल्माए गए जीवों को गिना। हर चार में से लगभग तीन जीव रोशनी बना सकते थे। वहाँ नीचे, बिना रोशनी वाला जीव ही अनोखा है।

गहरे समुद्र के जीव अपनी चमक से शिकार करते हैं, छिपते हैं, हमलावरों को चौंकाते हैं और अँधेरे में एक-दूसरे को ढूँढते हैं। मिसाल के लिए, लालटेन मछलियों के शरीर पर नन्ही बत्तियों की कतारें होती हैं, जिनका पैटर्न हर किस्म में अलग होता है। शायद इससे उन्हें अपनी ही [[species|प्रजाति]] के साथियों को पहचानने में मदद मिलती है।

कुछ जेलीफ़िश चोर-घंटी की तरह नीले छल्ले चमकाती हैं, ताकि बड़े जीव आ जाएँ और उन पर हमला करने वाले को खा जाएँ।
गहरे समुद्र के कुछ झींगे चमकते बादल थूकते हैं, ताकि शिकारी की आँखें चौंधिया जाएँ और वे भाग निकलें।
कुछ मछलियों के पेट पर बत्तियाँ होती हैं, जो ऊपर से आती हल्की रोशनी से मेल खाती हैं। नीचे से देखो तो वे गायब हो जाती हैं।

sec.t:
सबसे मशहूर चमकने वाली मछली है गहरे समुद्र की एंगलरफ़िश। मादा के सिर पर एक लंबा काँटा होता है, मछली पकड़ने की बंसी जैसा, और उसके सिरे पर एक चमकता बल्ब। यह रोशनी मछली खुद नहीं बनाती। यह बल्ब के अंदर रहने वाले चमकीले बैक्टीरिया से आती है।

छोटी मछलियाँ और झींगे रोशनी की तरफ़ तैरकर आते हैं, जैसे पतंगे स्ट्रीट लाइट के चारों ओर मँडराते हैं। एंगलरफ़िश इंतज़ार करती है, फिर सुई जैसे दाँतों से भरा मुँह खोलती है और गप्प से निगल जाती है।

एंगलरफ़िश की कुछ किस्मों में नर बहुत छोटे होते हैं। जब नर को कोई मादा मिलती है, तो वह उससे दाँत गड़ाकर चिपक जाता है और फिर कभी नहीं छोड़ता। धीरे-धीरे उसका शरीर मादा के शरीर से जुड़ जाता है, और वह उसके बगल में एक छोटे-से उभार की तरह ज़िंदा रहता है।

गहरे समुद्र की ज़्यादातर रोशनी नीली या नीली-हरी होती है। नीली रोशनी समुद्र के पानी में सबसे दूर तक जाती है, जबकि लाल रोशनी कुछ ही मीटर में ख़त्म हो जाती है। इसी वजह से गहरे समुद्र की ज़्यादातर आँखें बस नीला ही देख पाती हैं।

एक मछली यह नियम तोड़ती है। स्टॉपलाइट लूसजॉ, जो ड्रैगनफ़िश की एक किस्म है, अपनी आँख के नीचे से लाल रोशनी फेंकती है। वहाँ नीचे लगभग कोई और लाल रंग नहीं देख पाता, इसलिए वह अपने शिकार पर रोशनी डाल सकती है और किसी को पता भी नहीं चलता।

कुछ जीव गायब होने के लिए चमकते हैं। हैचेटफ़िश के पेट पर बत्तियाँ होती हैं, जो ऊपर से आती हल्की चमक से मेल खाती हैं। नीचे से देखने पर उनकी काली परछाईं गायब हो जाती है। वैज्ञानिक इसे काउंटर-इल्यूमिनेशन कहते हैं, जो एक तरह का [[@camouflage|कैमूफ़्लाज]] है।

अमेरिका की समुद्र वैज्ञानिक एडिथ विडर ने अपनी पूरी ज़िंदगी चमकने वाले जीवों के अध्ययन में लगाई है। उन्होंने देखा कि अटोला नाम की गहरे समुद्र की एक जेलीफ़िश पर हमला होता है, तो वह नीली रोशनी का एक घूमता छल्ला चमकाती है। उनका अनुमान था कि यह चमक चोर-घंटी की तरह काम करती है, जो बड़े शिकारियों को बुलाती है ताकि वे हमलावर को खा जाएँ।

तो उन्होंने नीली बत्तियों से एक नकली जेलीफ़िश बनाई, जिसे "ई-जेली" नाम दिया गया, ताकि वह उसी घंटी की नकल करे। 2012 में जापान के पास एक [[expedition|खोजी अभियान]] में इसी ई-जेली ने एक [[@giant-squid|विशाल स्क्विड]] को अपनी ओर खींचा। पहली बार कैमरों ने गहरे समुद्र में उसके घर में एक ज़िंदा विशाल स्क्विड को फ़िल्माया।

बायोल्यूमिनेसेंस देखने के लिए पनडुब्बी की ज़रूरत नहीं। कुछ रातों में भारत के समुद्र तटों पर, [[@mumbai|मुंबई]] के जुहू से लेकर चेन्नई तक, लहरें बिजली जैसी नीली चमकती हैं। यह रोशनी "सी स्पार्कल" नाम के एक नन्हे, पानी में बहते जीव से आती है, जो पानी हिलते ही चमक उठता है। [[@puerto-rico|प्यूर्टो रिको]] की मॉस्किटो बे इतनी तेज़ चमकती है कि चप्पू चलाओ तो पानी में रोशनी की लकीर बन जाती है।

ज़मीन पर [[@fireflies|जुगनू]] लगभग यही रासायनिक तरकीब अपनाते हैं। वैज्ञानिकों ने तो एक जेलीफ़िश से चमकने वाला एक [[protein|प्रोटीन]] उधार लेकर प्रयोगशाला में कोशिकाओं को रोशन कर दिखाया है। जिन लोगों ने इसके इस्तेमाल का तरीका खोजा, उन्हें 2008 का रसायन का नोबेल पुरस्कार मिला।

text: Most scientists would hand the title to the tardigrade. It is a plump, eight-legged animal usually less than 1 mm long, about the size of a grain of salt. It waddles slowly through water films on moss, which is why people call it a water bear.

When its home dries up, a tardigrade pulls in its head and legs, loses almost all its water and curls into a dry ball called a tun. In that state it can survive deep freezing, boiling heat, crushing pressure and blasts of [[radiation|radiation]] that would kill a person many times over.

st.reveal: Tardigrades live almost everywhere, from mountain tops to the deep sea. The easiest place to find them is in moss or lichen, where a thin film of water gives them room to crawl.

d.try: Go tardigrade hunting with an adult. Collect a small clump of dry moss, soak it in a dish of rainwater overnight, then squeeze the water into a clear lid. Look with a strong magnifying glass or a cheap clip-on phone microscope for slow, chubby, eight-legged crawlers.
myth: Tardigrades are indestructible and can survive anything at any time.
They are only super-tough when dried out into a tun. An active, wet tardigrade is fragile. Studies show a few days at about 37°C, the temperature of your body, is enough to kill many of them.

sec.t:
Living things need water to run the chemistry of life. Tardigrades can lose about 97% of theirs. Their bodies fill up with special sugars and [[protein|proteins]] that hold cells in shape, a bit like packing glass in bubble wrap.

In the tun state, their life processes slow to less than 0.01% of normal. They are not quite dead, but not really living either. Add water and, within minutes to hours, they puff back up and start walking.

sec.h: Into space and onto the Moon
sec.t:
In 2007, a European experiment called TARDIS put dried tardigrades on the outside of a satellite for 10 days. They faced the airless [[vacuum|vacuum]] of space and the Sun's harsh radiation. Back on Earth, some woke up, and a few later laid eggs that hatched.

In 2019, an Israeli lander named Beresheet crashed onto the Moon carrying thousands of dried tardigrades. Nobody knows if any survived. Later, scientists fired tuns from a special gun at a target. They died when they hit faster than about 900 m per second. A hard crash on the Moon was probably too much even for them.

In 1983, Japanese scientists collected moss in Antarctica and stored it in a freezer at −20°C. In 2014, they thawed it. Two tardigrades woke up, after more than 30 years on ice. One laid eggs, and the babies hatched healthy.

Tardigrades are not alone. Tiny animals called bdelloid rotifers were revived in 2021 after about 24,000 years frozen in the Siberian [[permafrost|permafrost]]. The [[@power-wood-frog|wood frog]] of North America lets its body freeze solid in winter, its heart stopping until spring.

The [[@power-naked-mole-rat|naked mole-rat]] is another kind of tough. It can live more than 30 years, almost never gets cancer and survives about 18 minutes with no oxygen at all.

Tardigrades were first described in 1773 by a German pastor, Johann Goeze, who peered at them through an early [[microscope|microscope]] and called them little water bears. Today scientists study them to learn how to protect things that hate drying out, from [[vaccine|vaccines]] that need no fridge to future astronauts' bodies. Their DNA-shielding protein has already been tested in human cells in the lab.

They also change how we think about [[@alien-life|alien life]]. An animal smaller than a grain of salt can ride outside a satellite and wake up later. So life elsewhere in the universe might be far harder to kill than we once thought.

text: The tallest building on Earth is the Burj Khalifa in [[@dubai|Dubai]], which reaches 828 metres. That is about two and a half Eiffel Towers stacked up, or more than four Statues of Unity. It opened in 2010 and has 163 floors. On a clear day its tip can be seen from about 95 kilometres away.

Next comes Merdeka 118 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, at 679 metres. The tallest tower, meaning a structure people don't live or work in, is the Tokyo Skytree at 634 metres. The record may not last. In Saudi Arabia, the Jeddah Tower had climbed past 100 floors by mid-2026 and is planned to reach about 1,008 metres, the first building a kilometre high.

st.reveal: The Great Pyramid, about 146 metres tall when new, held the record for roughly 3,800 years. The Eiffel Tower held it for about 41 years, and the Empire State Building for less than that.

sec.t:
Around 2560 BCE, Egyptian builders finished the [[@pyramids|Great Pyramid]] of Giza for the pharaoh Khufu. It stood about 146 metres tall, roughly a 45-storey block. No human-made structure beat it for about 3,800 years. The first to do so was probably the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England, finished around 1311. It blew down in a storm in 1548.

In India, the [[@qutub-minar|Qutub Minar]] in Delhi rose to about 73 metres in the 1200s and is still one of the tallest brick towers anywhere.

The biggest enemy of a tall building isn't [[gravity|gravity]]. It's wind. Air pushes against the side, and vortices, swirls of wind peeling off the corners, can make a tower rock back and forth. The Burj Khalifa's Y-shaped base and stepped sides break those swirls up. Taipei 101 in Taiwan hangs a steel ball weighing about 660 tonnes near its top. When the building sways one way, the ball swings the other and calms it.

Lifts are another headache. Steel lift ropes get so heavy over very long runs that the tallest buildings use "sky lobbies", where you change lifts partway up, like changing trains.

India's tallest buildings are mostly in Mumbai, where land is scarce and expensive, and several towers there rise well above 250 metres. In 2022 a pair of illegally built towers in Noida, near Delhi, set a different kind of record. The two buildings, about 100 metres tall, were brought down by controlled explosions in roughly nine seconds.

Building tall in India means planning for [[monsoon|monsoon]] storms, and in the north for earthquakes, so engineers test models of big towers in wind tunnels before work begins.

sec.h: Masts, statues and the one that fell
sec.t:
Some of the tallest things ever built are thin masts held up by steel cables. In North Dakota, USA, a TV mast called KVLY rises about 629 metres. A taller one, the Warsaw radio mast in Poland, reached 646 metres. In 1991, during work on its cables, it bent and crashed to the ground.

Statues have grown too. The [[@statue-of-unity|Statue of Unity]] in Gujarat, showing Sardar Patel, opened in 2018 at 182 metres, about twice the height of the Statue of Liberty with its base. And the next giant is already on the way: engineers in Jeddah are learning to make [[@skyscrapers|skyscrapers]] behave at heights nobody has ever tried.

text: A stepwell is a deep well with flights of steps leading down to the water. In the dry parts of western India, the water underground rises after the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] and sinks during the long, hot months that follow. A normal well with a rope and bucket works only if the rope is long enough. With steps, people could simply walk down to wherever the water was.

Stepwells were dug into the ground until they reached [[@groundwater|groundwater]], the water stored in sand and rock below. Water seeped in from the sides and collected in a pool at the bottom. Many stepwells also caught rain flowing off the land around them. Over time, builders turned them into works of art, with carved pillars, galleries and statues of gods.

st.reveal: In dry regions, groundwater can fall many metres between the monsoon and the hottest months. Steps let people walk down to wherever the water happened to be, all year round, without ropes or buckets.

Scoop some water out over a few days and watch the level drop. Now try building steps of clay or pebbles down the side so a toy figure could still reach it.

Many were paid for by queens and wealthy women, as well as merchants. Rani ki Vav means "the queen's stepwell", and the Adalaj stepwell was completed by a queen named Rudabai.

sec.t:
Builders began by digging a long trench. At one end, a round well shaft went straight down to the water. Along the trench, they built stone steps, landings and pillared floors, one below another, like an upside-down building.

The deepest stepwells go down the height of a ten-storey building. Thick stone walls held back the soil. Pillars and beams kept the walls from caving in. At the bottom, the air was shady and noticeably cooler than at the surface, so people rested there on summer afternoons.

Chand Baori, in the village of Abhaneri in [[@rajasthan-forts|Rajasthan]], is about 1,200 years old. Its roughly 3,500 steps form a dizzying pattern of zigzags on three sides, dropping about 13 levels to the water.

Rani ki Vav, at Patan in Gujarat, was built in the 11th century in memory of King Bhima I, and is linked to his queen, Udayamati. It is about 64 metres long and lined with hundreds of carved [[sculpture|sculptures]]. Floods from a nearby river later filled it with silt, which protected the carvings. After [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] cleared it, it became a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 2014.

The Adalaj stepwell near Ahmedabad, finished in 1499, has five storeys of carved balconies. Local stories say it was completed by Queen Rudabai. Its carvings mix Hindu and Jain designs with Islamic patterns, a reminder that it was begun under one ruler and finished under another.

Delhi has stepwells too. Agrasen ki Baoli, a tall, narrow stepwell with about 100 steps, stands among office towers near Connaught Place. Its exact age is unknown. On a hot afternoon, its lower steps are still a few degrees cooler than the street outside.

During British rule, officials worried that stepwells spread disease, because people bathed and drew drinking water from the same pool. Some were closed or filled in. Later, piped water, hand pumps and [[@wells-borewells|borewells]] meant few people needed the steps any more. Many stepwells filled with rubbish or were left to crumble.

In recent years, people have started to look at them again. Some cities have cleaned out old stepwells so they can catch rain and recharge the ground. Visitors now travel to see them, and photographers love their patterns of light and shadow. The lesson they teach is the same one behind modern rainwater harvesting: hold on to the [[monsoon|monsoon]] for as long as you can.

text: Every four years, in November, American citizens aged 18 and over vote for president. But they are not voting for the president directly. In each state, they are really choosing a group of people called electors.
Together, the electors from all 50 states and Washington, D.C., make up the Electoral College. There are 538 of them. Whoever wins at least 270 electoral votes becomes president.

In almost every state, the candidate who wins the most votes in that state gets all of its electors. That is why a candidate can win the most votes across the country and still lose, which has happened five times.

st.reveal: There are 538 electoral votes in total, shared among the states and Washington, D.C. A candidate needs more than half, which is 270. If nobody gets 270, the House of Representatives chooses.

sec.t:
The men who wrote the [[@us-constitution|US Constitution]] in 1787 argued for weeks about how to choose a president. Some wanted Congress to pick. Others wanted a direct vote by the people. Small states feared big states would always win.

The Electoral College was a compromise. Each state gets as many electors as it has members of Congress: one for each of its seats in the House of Representatives, plus two for its two senators. Washington, D.C., got three electors in 1961. California has the most, with 54. Small states such as Wyoming have three.

On Election Day, people vote at schools, churches and libraries, and many states let people vote early or by post. News organisations count results through the night and project winners state by state.

A few states, called swing states, could go either way and get most of the attention. Others reliably vote for one party year after year.

In December, the electors meet in their states and cast their votes. Congress counts them in January, and the new president is sworn in on 20 January, usually on the steps of the Capitol in [[@washington-dc|Washington, D.C.]]

At first, in most states, only white men who owned property could vote. Over time, [[@constitution-amendments|amendments]] to the Constitution widened the vote. The 15th Amendment (1870) said race could not be used to stop men voting, though many states found unfair ways around it for almost a century. The 19th Amendment (1920) gave women the vote. The 26th Amendment (1971) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18.

Today, citizens must usually register before voting, and each state sets its own rules for how.

India's top leader, the prime minister, is not elected directly either. Voters choose Members of [[@parliament-india|Parliament]], and the party or group with a majority in the [[@lok-sabha-rajya-sabha|Lok Sabha]] forms the government. India's president is elected by MPs and members of state assemblies.

Americans have debated the Electoral College for a long time. Supporters say it makes candidates pay attention to smaller states and rural areas, and keeps the states important. Critics say every person's vote should count equally across the country, and that the national winner should always win. Changing it would need a constitutional [[amendment|amendment]], which is very hard to pass.

text: A bank keeps your money safe and lets you take it out when you need it. But it does not just store it. A bank takes money deposited by many people and lends most of it to others: families buying houses, farmers buying seeds, businesses building factories.

Borrowers pay the bank [[interest|interest]], an extra charge for using the money. The bank pays a smaller amount of interest to people who deposited, and keeps the difference to cover its costs and make a profit. So when your savings grow in a bank account, it is partly because someone else is paying to borrow money.

st.reveal: Banks keep only a slice as cash and reserves, enough for normal withdrawals. The rest is lent out to people and businesses who pay interest, which is how banks earn money and pay you interest too.

d.try: Set up a "family bank" with a jar and a notebook. When you deposit money, write it down. Agree with an adult on a small "interest" reward each month, like one extra rupee for every ten saved. Watch how your balance grows faster the longer you leave it.
myth: The bank keeps your money locked in a vault with your name on it.

Your money is mixed with everyone else's and most of it is lent out. What the bank keeps is a record that it owes you that amount. Deposit insurance and strict rules make sure you can still get it back.

sec.t:
On any normal day, only a few customers want their cash back. So a bank keeps a slice of its deposits as cash and reserves, and lends out the rest. In India, the Reserve Bank of India sets rules for how much banks must keep aside. This is called fractional reserve banking, because only a fraction is held back.

It works as long as people trust the bank. If everyone rushes to withdraw at once, a bank can run short of cash. That is called a bank run, and it has happened many times in history.

After many American banks failed during the Great Depression of the 1930s, the US government created the FDIC in 1933 to [[@insurance|insure deposits]]. Today, if an insured US bank fails, customers get back up to 250,000 dollars. In India, the DICGC insures deposits up to ₹5 lakh per person in each bank.

People have stored and lent valuables for thousands of years. In ancient [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], temples and palaces stored grain and silver and made loans. In India, moneylenders called sahukars and banking families lent money to traders and kings for centuries.

Modern banking grew in Italian cities like Florence and [[@venice|Venice]] in the 1300s and 1400s. Moneychangers sat at benches, or *banchi*, in the market. The Medici family of Florence became rich bankers and spent huge sums on art and buildings during the [[@renaissance|Renaissance]].

Banks also do many smaller jobs. They change foreign [[currency|currency]] for travellers, keep valuables in lockers, send money abroad, and give out debit and credit cards. Many now offer most of these services through phone apps, so customers rarely need to visit a branch.

Without banks, a young couple might have to save for 30 years before buying a home, and a small business could not buy a new machine until it had saved every rupee. Loans let people do things now and pay later. That also carries risk. Borrowers who take on too much debt can struggle to pay it back, and the interest keeps adding up. Banks check whether a borrower can repay before lending. Understanding how interest works, which you can explore in [[@money-maths|money maths]], is one of the most useful things anyone can learn.

text: Plenty of children and teenagers have changed the world. Some invented things, like Louis Braille, who created a reading system for blind people at 15. Some stood up to unfair rules, like Claudette Colvin and Ruby Bridges in the USA. Some spoke out for education, like Malala Yousafzai in Pakistan, or for the planet, like Greta Thunberg in Sweden.
They didn't have money or power. What they had was a problem they couldn't ignore and the stubbornness to keep going. Several were also helped by brave parents, teachers and friends.

st.reveal: Braille had lost his sight as a small child and was a student at a school for blind children in Paris. He shaped his six-dot code at about 15, in 1824, and kept improving it for years after.

sec.t:
In 1955, buses in Montgomery, Alabama, made Black passengers give up seats to white passengers. On 2 March that year, a 15-year-old schoolgirl, Claudette Colvin, refused. She was arrested. Nine months later, [[@rosa-parks|Rosa Parks]] did the same, and her arrest sparked a famous bus boycott. Colvin later became one of the young people whose court case helped end bus segregation.

In 1960, six-year-old [[@usa-ruby-bridges|Ruby Bridges]] became the first Black child at William Frantz Elementary, an all-white primary school in New Orleans. [[federal|Federal]] officers walked her past angry crowds every day. For most of that year she was the only child in her class.

sec.h: Marching for the right to be a child
sec.t:
In 1903, many American children worked long hours in cotton mills instead of going to school. The campaigner Mary Harris Jones, known as Mother Jones, led a march of child workers and adults from Philadelphia towards the New York home of President Theodore Roosevelt. He refused to meet them. But newspapers covered the march, and it helped build support for laws against [[@child-labour|child labour]].

In India, the fight against child labour carries on. Kailash Satyarthi, who shared the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize with Malala, has spent decades rescuing children from factories.

sec.h: A schoolgirl, a blog and a Nobel Prize
sec.t: Malala Yousafzai grew up in the Swat Valley of Pakistan. At 11, she began writing a blog about life under a group that banned girls from school. In 2012, at 15, she was attacked on her school bus because of her campaign. She survived and kept speaking out. In 2014, at 17, she became the youngest person ever to win a Nobel Prize.

Some young changemakers break limits. In May 2014, Malavath Purna from a village in Telangana reached the top of Mount Everest at 13. She became the youngest girl to climb it, about 60 years after the [[@everest-first|first climbers]] stood there.

In 2018, 15-year-old Greta Thunberg started sitting outside the Swedish [[parliament|parliament]] on school days, holding a sign about [[climate|climate]] change. Within a year, millions of students in many countries had joined school strikes. In 2020, Gitanjali Rao, a 15-year-old Indian-American from Colorado, was named TIME magazine's first Kid of the Year. She had built a small device to test drinking water for lead.

Children have also invented everyday things, from earmuffs to the ice lolly, as the story of [[@inventions-kids|inventions by kids]] shows.

text: Reservation is India's system of setting aside a share of places for groups that faced discrimination for a very long time. It applies to government jobs, seats in public colleges, and seats in Parliament, state assemblies and village councils.

The main groups are Scheduled Castes, communities once treated as "untouchable" under the [[@caste-history|caste system]], and Scheduled Tribes, many of them [[indigenous|Adivasi]] communities. Other Backward Classes and, since 2019, poorer families outside these groups have reserved places too. The idea is that equal rules are not enough when some people start the race far behind the line.

st.reveal: Only Scheduled Caste candidates can stand in that seat, but every adult in the area votes. The winner has to win support across the whole community, which was part of the idea.

sec.t:
Reserved shares for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes roughly follow their share of the population. In central government jobs and colleges, that means 15% and 7.5%.

In 1980 the Mandal Commission recommended reservation for Other Backward Classes, a large group of castes that were poor but not "untouchable". When the government brought in 27% for them in 1990, there were huge protests, especially by students. In 1992 the Supreme Court upheld the policy, but said reservation should usually not go above half of all places. It also said the better-off families within these groups, called the "creamy layer", should not benefit.

In 2019, a constitutional [[amendment|amendment]] added 10% for poorer families from groups that had no reservation before.

In practice, take a public engineering college that fills its seats through one national exam. Everyone sits the same paper. The open seats go to the top scorers of any background, and the reserved seats go to the top scorers within each category. Many states run their own reservation lists for state jobs and colleges, with different shares, so the rules in Tamil Nadu are not the same as those in Punjab.

One form of reservation has changed rural India quietly. Since 1993, at least a third of seats in [[@panchayat|panchayats]] must go to women, and many states have raised this to half. As a result, lakhs of women now serve as village councillors and sarpanches. In 2023 Parliament passed a law to reserve a third of Lok Sabha and assembly seats for women. It is due to take effect after a new [[census|census]] and a redrawing of constituencies.

Supporters point out that caste still shapes who gets good jobs, who owns land and who is treated with respect. They say reservation has created teachers, doctors and officers from families that had none, and that it is still needed.

Critics argue that seats should go by merit alone, or by income instead of caste. Others worry that benefits go mostly to the better-off families within each group. In 2024 the Supreme Court allowed states to divide reserved quotas into sub-groups, partly for this reason.

Other countries face similar questions. The United States used affirmative action in college admissions for decades, until its Supreme Court ended race-conscious admissions in 2023.

text: A runoff is a second round of voting. If no candidate wins more than half the votes in the first round, the top two go head to head a few weeks later.
Because only two remain, whoever wins the runoff is sure to have the support of more than half of the people who voted in it.

news.t: On 25 October 2026, Brazil held a runoff for president because no candidate won more than half the votes in the first round on 4 October. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won just over 51% against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro's 48%, giving him a fourth term. This entry explains how runoff elections work.

sec.t:
When many candidates stand, the votes can split. Someone might come first with only 30%, even if most voters would have preferred someone else. A runoff makes sure the winner has the backing of a majority, more than 50%.

Between rounds, candidates try to win over the voters whose favourite was knocked out. So a runoff often rewards the candidate who can appeal to the widest range of people, not just the most loyal fans.

In [[@elections-india|India's elections]], each seat is won by whoever gets the most votes, even if that is less than half. This is called first past the post. It is simple, fast and needs only one round, which matters when [[@vote-how|crores of people vote]].

Different countries choose different rules, and each has fans and critics. The USA uses yet another system, with an [[@elections-usa|Electoral College]]. Whether a country has a [[@president-pm|president or a prime minister]] also changes what is being voted for. All of these systems are built on one idea, using [[@percentages|percentages]] of votes to turn many choices into one decision, the heart of a [[democracy|democracy]].

sec.t:
शरीर की घड़ी अपने-आप एकदम सही नहीं चलती। ज़्यादातर लोगों में यह थोड़ी सुस्त चलती है, यानी इसका कुदरती चक्र 24 घंटे से ज़रा लंबा होता है। रोशनी इसे ठीक करती है। आँख के पिछले हिस्से में, [[retina|रेटिना]] में, कुछ खास कोशिकाएँ रोशनी को भाँपती हैं और सीधे मुख्य घड़ी तक संकेत भेजती हैं।

सुबह की रोशनी दिमाग को बताती है कि दिन शुरू हो गया। शाम को जब रोशनी ढलती है, तो दिमाग की एक [[gland|ग्रंथि]] मेलाटोनिन छोड़ने लगती है। यह एक [[hormone|हॉर्मोन]] है जिससे नींद आने लगती है। देर रात चमकती स्क्रीन इसे टाल सकती है। यही एक वजह है कि डॉक्टर सोने से पहले स्क्रीन बंद करने को कहते हैं, जैसा [[@screen-time|स्क्रीन नींद के साथ क्या करती है]] में समझाया गया है।

हमें कैसे पता कि यह घड़ी अपने-आप चलती है? पहला सुराग पौधों से मिला। 1729 में फ़्रांस के वैज्ञानिक ज़्याँ-ज़ाक दोर्तू द मेरां ने मिमोसा का एक पौधा, जो छुईमुई के परिवार का है, एक अँधेरी अलमारी में रख दिया। उसकी पत्तियाँ रोज़ ऐसे खुलती-बंद होती रहीं, मानो सूरज अब भी उग रहा हो।

1938 में दो अमेरिकी वैज्ञानिक, नैथेनियल क्लाइटमैन और ब्रूस रिचर्डसन, अमेरिका के केंटकी राज्य की मैमथ गुफ़ा की गहराई में 32 दिन तक रहे। वे 28 घंटे के दिन पर जीने की कोशिश कर रहे थे। रिचर्डसन का शरीर कुछ हद तक ढल गया, पर क्लाइटमैन का शरीर ज़िद करके लगभग 24 घंटे पर ही अड़ा रहा।

1962 में फ़्रांस के एक युवा गुफ़ा खोजी, मिशेल सिफ़्र, ज़मीन के नीचे की एक गुफ़ा में बिना घड़ी के लगभग दो महीने अकेले रहे। उनकी सोने-जागने की कुदरती लय बनी रही, पर जब वे बाहर आए, तो उन्हें लगा कि असल से बहुत कम दिन बीते हैं।

कोशिकाएँ समय कैसे रखती हैं? फलों पर मँडराने वाली नन्ही मक्खियों पर शोध कर रहे वैज्ञानिकों को ऐसे [[gene|जीन]] मिले जो एक प्रोटीन बनाते हैं। यह प्रोटीन रात में कोशिकाओं में जमा होता है और दिन में टूट जाता है, और यह पूरा चक्र लगभग 24 घंटे में घूमता है। यह गुत्थी सुलझाने के लिए जेफ़री हॉल, माइकल रॉसबैश और माइकल यंग को 2017 में चिकित्सा का नोबेल पुरस्कार मिला।

ऐसी ही घड़ियाँ तुम्हारे शरीर की लगभग हर कोशिका में टिक-टिक करती हैं। दिमाग की मुख्य घड़ी सबको एक ताल में रखती है, जैसे ऑर्केस्ट्रा को चलाने वाला संचालक।

अगर तुम मुंबई से न्यूयॉर्क उड़कर जाओ, तो वहाँ सूरज उस समय उगता है जिसे तुम्हारा शरीर शाम समझता है। तुम्हारी घड़ी को नए समय से तालमेल बिठाने में कई दिन लगते हैं। इसे [[@jet-lag|जेट लैग]] कहते हैं। नर्सों और पायलटों जैसे रात की पाली में काम करने वालों को भी अपने शरीर की घड़ी से जूझना पड़ता है।

नींद के जानकारों के अनुसार 6 से 12 साल के बच्चों को हर रात लगभग 9 से 12 घंटे की नींद चाहिए। रोज़ लगभग एक ही समय पर सोना और उठना, और सुबह थोड़ी धूप लेना, तुम्हारी घड़ी को ठीक-ठाक चलाए रखता है।

sec.t:
मांसपेशियाँ लंबी कोशिकाओं से बनी हैं, जिन्हें रेशे कहते हैं। इनके भीतर [[protein|प्रोटीन]] के नन्हे धागे एक-दूसरे पर सरकते हैं और मांसपेशी को छोटा कर देते हैं। मांसपेशी सिर्फ़ खींच सकती है। बाँह मोड़ने के लिए बाइसेप्स खींचती है। उसे सीधा करने के लिए एक दूसरी मांसपेशी, ट्राइसेप्स, उल्टी तरफ़ खींचती है।

बड़ी मांसपेशियों में ज़्यादा रेशे अगल-बगल काम करते हैं, इसलिए वे ज़्यादा ज़ोर से खींच सकती हैं। अभ्यास से रेशे मोटे होते हैं। यह [[neuron|तंत्रिका तंत्र]] को एक साथ ज़्यादा रेशे चालू करना भी सिखाता है। इसीलिए नौसिखिए मांसपेशियाँ बड़ी दिखने से बहुत पहले ही जल्दी ताकतवर हो जाते हैं।

जुलाई 2021 में मणिपुर की मीराबाई चानू ने टोक्यो 2020 ओलंपिक में महिलाओं के 49 किलो वर्ग में भारत को रजत पदक दिलाया। उन्होंने दो लिफ़्ट में कुल 202 किलो उठाया, अपने वज़न का लगभग चार गुना।

छोटे भारोत्तोलक अक्सर अपने आकार के हिसाब से ज़्यादा उठाते हैं। ताकत मांसपेशी की मोटाई, यानी उसके कटे हुए सिरे के क्षेत्रफल पर निर्भर है, और जानवर जैसे-जैसे बड़े होते हैं, यह शरीर के वज़न से धीमे बढ़ती है। इसीलिए अपने आकार के मुकाबले चींटियाँ और भृंग चैंपियन हैं। गोबर के भृंग की एक किस्म अपने वज़न से हज़ार गुना से भी ज़्यादा खींच सकती है। अगर कोई इंसान अपने वज़न का हज़ार गुना ढोए, तो वह पूरी लदी हुई मालगाड़ी उठाए खड़ा होगा।

वैज्ञानिकों ने बिजली के हल्के झटकों से मांसपेशियों को उत्तेजित करके नापा, और पाया कि वे उससे ज़्यादा ज़ोर से खींच सकती हैं जितना लोग अपनी मर्ज़ी से कर पाते हैं। लगता है दिमाग आम तौर पर कुछ ताकत रोककर रखता है।

किस्से सुनाए जाते हैं कि किसी ने किसी की जान बचाने के लिए कार उठा ली। ज़्यादातर मामलों में पता चलता है कि उन्होंने एक कोना या एक तरफ़ उठाई थी, जो पूरी कार उठाने से कहीं आसान है। एड्रेनलिन, जो डर या जोश में छूटने वाला एक [[hormone|हॉर्मोन]] है, शायद थोड़ी मदद करता है। मुसीबत में लोग असल में कितनी ज़्यादा ताकत जुटा सकते हैं, इसे सुरक्षित ढंग से परखना मुश्किल है।

बच्चे और किशोर पुश-अप, उठक-बैठक जैसी स्क्वैट और चढ़ाई जैसी अपने वज़न वाली कसरतों से, और किसी बड़े की निगरानी में हल्के वज़न से, सुरक्षित ढंग से ताकत बढ़ा सकते हैं। हड्डियाँ और [[@muscles|मांसपेशियाँ]] बीस-पच्चीस की उम्र तक बढ़ती रहती हैं। ताकत वाली कसरत हड्डियों को और ठोस भी बनाती है, जो ज़िंदगी भर काम आता है। अंतरिक्ष यात्री उल्टी वजह से अंतरिक्ष में हड्डियों की ताकत गँवाते हैं: धकेलने को कोई वज़न न हो, तो हड्डियाँ कमज़ोर हो जाती हैं। फिर भी, अपने आकार के हिसाब से कच्ची ताकत में कोई इंसान [[@extreme-strongest-animals|सबसे ताकतवर जानवरों]] के आसपास भी नहीं पहुँचता, गोबर के भृंग से लेकर गैंडा भृंग तक।

text: Rome grew from a small town in central Italy into one of the largest [[empire|empires]] in history. It did this over hundreds of years with a powerful army, a habit of turning defeated enemies into allies, and very practical engineering: roads, [[@bridges|bridges]], [[aqueduct|aqueducts]] and concrete.

Rome also offered something to the peoples it conquered. Local leaders who cooperated could become Roman citizens, enjoy Roman law and trade across the empire. Many cities came to see themselves as Roman. That loyalty helped the empire last for centuries.

st.reveal: Pepper from the Malabar coast of Kerala was so prized in Rome that warehouses were built just to store it. Romans had never heard of tea, and potatoes grew only in South America until the 1500s.

sec.t:
Legend says Rome was founded in 753 BCE by Romulus and Remus, twin brothers raised by a she-wolf. For about 250 years, kings ruled. Then, in 509 BCE, the Romans threw out their last king and set up a [[republic|republic]]. Two leaders called consuls were elected each year, advised by a council of older men, the Senate.

The republic conquered Italy, then fought [[@carthage|Carthage]], a rich trading city in North Africa. The Carthaginian general Hannibal famously marched [[@oddity-elephants-war|war elephants]] over the Alps, but Rome won in the end. After years of civil war, Julius Caesar took power and was murdered in 44 BCE. His adopted son Octavian became the first emperor, Augustus, in 27 BCE.

Rome's soldiers were trained professionals. A legion had about 5,000 men, organised into smaller units with clear ranks. They drilled constantly, marched about 30 km in a day carrying heavy packs, and built a fortified camp each night.

Wherever the army went, it built [[@roman-roads|roads]] to move troops and supplies quickly. Soldiers who served 25 years were given land or money, and non-citizen soldiers received citizenship. In 212 CE, Emperor Caracalla made almost all free people in the empire Roman citizens.

Romans mixed lime with volcanic ash to make a concrete that could even set underwater. With it they built harbours, domes and the arches of the [[@colosseum|Colosseum]]. Aqueducts carried fresh water for kilometres into cities, mostly by gentle slopes underground. Rome itself had public baths, fountains and [[@oddity-ancient-toilets|toilets]] flushed by running water.

{{story:roman-numerals}}

Roman ships sailed from Egypt across the Arabian Sea, riding [[@monsoon|the monsoon]] winds, to ports on India's west coast. One of the most important was Muziris, in today's [[@kerala|Kerala]]. They brought gold and silver coins, wine and glass, and took home [[@food-pepper-black-gold|pepper]] and other [[@spices|spices]], pearls, ivory and fine [[@clothes-cotton|cotton]] cloth.

Hoards of Roman coins have been dug up across South India. At Arikamedu, near [[@puducherry|Puducherry]], [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] found Roman pottery and wine jars. The writer Pliny the Elder grumbled that India drained Rome of vast sums every year in exchange for luxuries.

By the 200s CE, the empire was huge and hard to defend. Emperors came and went quickly, often murdered by their own soldiers. Taxes rose, money lost its value, and groups from outside the borders pressed in. The empire was split into eastern and western halves.

In 476 CE, a Germanic general removed the last western emperor. The eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, now [[@istanbul|Istanbul]], carried on for nearly 1,000 more years, until 1453.

[[@latin-roots|Latin]], the Roman language, grew into Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian, and gave English thousands of words. July and August are named after Julius Caesar and Augustus. The USA named its Senate after Rome's, and the US Capitol takes its name from Rome's Capitoline Hill. Clock faces and book chapters still use [[@roman-numerals|Roman numerals]], more than 1,500 years after the last western emperor.

text: India has a long history of spies, going back more than 2,000 years. The Arthashastra, a book about statecraft linked to [[@chanakya|Chanakya]], describes networks of secret agents watching the kingdom and its enemies. Later rulers, from the Mughals to [[@tipu-sultan|Tipu Sultan]], kept their own news-gatherers and messengers.

Some of the most famous Indian spies lived in the last 200 years. A group of Himalayan explorers mapped Tibet in disguise. Noor Inayat Khan, an Indian-origin woman, worked as a secret radio operator in Paris during the Second World War. Teenagers joined spy units in the struggle for independence. Most of the stories of modern spies are still secret.

sec.h: A spy manual from ancient India
sec.t:
The Arthashastra gives kings very detailed advice. It describes spies disguised as wandering monks, traders, students, farmers and even fortune-tellers. Some were to stay in one place for years, and others were to travel and report back.

The book also talks about using signals and hidden messages so that spies couldn't be caught with letters. Scholars argue over exactly when it was written and by whom. Many think it was put together over several centuries, with its earliest parts more than 2,000 years old.

Noor Inayat Khan was born in Moscow in 1914 to an Indian father, a Sufi musician, and was a [[descendant|descendant]] of Tipu Sultan. She grew up in Paris and London, and wrote children's stories. During the Second World War she joined a secret British organisation that sent agents into German-held France.

In 1943 she became the first woman radio operator sent into occupied France. With other agents arrested, she kept sending messages to London alone for months, moving her radio from flat to flat. She was eventually betrayed and captured, and died in a prison camp in 1944. Britain awarded her its George Cross for bravery, and in 2020 she became the first woman of Indian origin honoured with a blue plaque in London.

During the freedom struggle, Subhas Chandra Bose's [[@indian-national-army|Indian National Army]] fought the British in Southeast Asia. Saraswathi Rajamani, a girl from a Tamil family in Burma, joined its intelligence wing at about 16. She cut her hair short and dressed as a boy named Mani to collect information from British camps. In one famous episode, she went back in disguise to help free a captured fellow agent.

India's Intelligence Bureau traces its roots back to 1887, which makes it one of the oldest intelligence services in the world. In 1968, India set up the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW) to gather information from abroad. Its founding chief, R. N. Kao, was famously private and rarely photographed.

Modern spies use satellites, computers and code-breaking as well as people. And the strangest part? One of the biggest spy victories of the Second World War was won by puzzle-solvers who cracked the [[@codes-enigma|Enigma code]], and no one was allowed to talk about it for 30 years.

text: The USA began in 1787 with 13 states along the Atlantic coast. Over the next 172 years it added 37 more, by buying land, signing [[treaty|treaties]], fighting wars and drawing new borders. The last two, Alaska and Hawaii, joined in 1959.

The rules came early. In 1787 Congress passed the Northwest Ordinance, which said new [[territory|territories]] could become full states, equal to the old ones, once enough people lived there. That promise turned a strip of coastal colonies into a country stretching 4,500 km across a continent, and then into the Pacific.

st.prompt: In 1867 the USA bought Alaska from Russia. Roughly how much did it pay per acre?
st.reveal: The USA paid about 7.2 million dollars for roughly 1.5 million square km, which works out to around 2 cents an acre. Some newspapers mocked it as "Seward's Folly", until gold rushes in and around Alaska in the 1880s and 1890s.

Almost every part of it was already home to Native American nations, and to Mexican, Hawaiian and other peoples. Much of the land changed hands through wars and broken treaties.

sec.t:
In 1803 the young USA wanted to buy one city, New Orleans, from France. The French ruler, Napoleon, needed money for his wars and offered something huge instead: the entire Louisiana territory. It cost about 15 million dollars and roughly doubled the size of the country overnight.

Parts of 15 future states came from that one deal. President Thomas Jefferson sent [[@lewis-clark|Lewis and Clark]] to explore it, though Native nations had lived there for thousands of years. Later, Texas joined after being its own independent [[republic|republic]] for nine years, from 1836 to 1845. A war with Mexico then brought in California and the Southwest.

California became a state in 1850, just two years after gold was found there. The [[@gold-rush|gold rush]] brought so many people so fast that it skipped the usual long wait as a territory. Railways and wagon trails pulled settlers further west, and new states followed: Oregon, Kansas, Nevada, Colorado.

Every new state stirred up a fierce question: would slavery be allowed there? The fight over the balance between free and slave states grew so bitter that it helped spark the Civil War in 1861. During that war, West Virginia split away from Virginia and became a state of its own.

Some borders were drawn with a ruler on a map, often by people who had never seen the land. That is why Colorado and Wyoming are almost perfect rectangles. Others follow rivers, like the Mississippi between several states. In the Southwest, four states meet at a single point called Four Corners. A visitor can put a hand or foot in each of them at the same time.

{{story:states-india}}

The map grew at a terrible cost to the people already on it. [[@native-nations|Native nations]] were pushed off their lands, often by force, and many treaties promising them land were later broken. In the 1830s, tens of thousands of Cherokee and other people were forced to march west, a journey now called the Trail of Tears.

Hawaii was an independent kingdom until 1893, when American businessmen overthrew its queen. In 1993, Congress formally apologised for that. Historians today tell the story of statehood alongside these losses, because both are true at once.

The final mainland states, New Mexico and Arizona, joined in 1912. Arizona's date was 14 February, so it is sometimes called the Valentine State. Then the map stood still for almost 50 years.

Alaska became the 49th state in January 1959 and Hawaii the 50th in August. A teenager in Ohio, Robert Heft, had sewn a 50-star flag for a school project. By his own account his teacher gave it a B minus, then raised it after the government picked his design. It has flown since 4 July 1960.

Will there ever be a 51st star? Washington, DC and Puerto Rico have both held votes on the idea, but Congress has not agreed. Meanwhile, the cheapest state of all keeps surprising people. Russia sold it for pocket change, yet [[@alaska|Alaska]] turned out to hold gold, oil and a coastline longer than all the other states put together.

text: Kerala's snake boat races are contests between huge, narrow wooden boats called *chundan vallam*. Each boat is more than 30 metres long, about as long as three school buses, and carries over 100 people. Most are rowers. A few steer with long oars at the back, and a few sing or beat time.

The races take place on Kerala's lakes and rivers, mostly in August and September around the harvest festival of Onam. The most famous, the Nehru Trophy Boat Race on Punnamada Lake near Alappuzha, draws huge crowds every year.

st.reveal: Singers on board chant traditional boat songs called vanchipattu, and the rhythm speeds up as the race heats up. Rowers dip their oars on the beat, so the whole boat moves like one long animal.

sec.t:
A snake boat is long and thin, with a high, curved stern that rises out of the water at the back. Traditionally, it is built from a hardwood called *anjili*, or wild jack, by master carpenters who follow old rules for its size and shape. Building one can take months.

Each boat belongs to a village, and people treat it with great respect. Traditionally the wood is rubbed with a mixture that includes fish oil, to keep it slippery and waterproof. Some villages say only certain people may step aboard, and only barefoot.

A snake boat sits very low in the water, its sides only a little above the surface. Rowers almost touch the lake as they paddle. The long, narrow shape cuts drag, the push of water against the hull, so a well-timed crew shoots forward surprisingly fast. On a calm lake the boats look like they are skimming rather than floating.

sec.h: How an accident became a festival

sec.t:
On race day, rowers sit in pairs down the length of the boat, each with a short paddle. Singers chant *vanchipattu*, traditional boat songs. As the boats near the finish, the songs grow faster and louder, and the oars churn the water white.

It looks like a riot of splashes, but the timing is exact. If even a few rowers fall out of [[rhythm|rhythm]], the boat slows. Teams train for weeks before the season. In 2019 Kerala launched a Champions Boat League, a series of races across the state with the best teams competing, a little like a cricket league on water.

Not every race is about winning. On the Pampa River, the Aranmula boat race is linked to the Parthasarathy temple. Its boats, called *palliyodam*, are seen as sacred. They glide in pairs during the Onam season, carrying offerings, and crowds line the banks to watch more than to cheer a winner.

In Aranmula, villagers also prepare a huge feast called the *vallasadya* for the boat crews. It can include more than 60 dishes served on banana leaves, and hosts keep refilling plates whenever a rower asks.

Snake boats were once part of real naval battles between kingdoms in old Kerala, used to move warriors quickly through the backwaters. Today, races fill [[@kerala|Kerala]]'s waterways with music in the [[@onam-pongal|Onam season]]. And how a wooden boat with over 100 people inside stays afloat at all is a neat piece of physics explained in [[@floating-ships|why ships float]].

text: India's "toy trains" are small mountain railways built in British times to reach hill stations. The three most famous climb to Darjeeling in West Bengal, Ooty in Tamil Nadu and Shimla in Himachal Pradesh. Together they are a UNESCO World Heritage Site called the Mountain Railways of India.

Their tracks are narrow, their carriages are small and they crawl along, often at little more than jogging speed. That is the whole point. Big trains can't make tight turns or steep climbs. These little ones twist, loop and zigzag their way up thousands of metres, through forests, tea gardens and clouds.

sec.h: Darjeeling: the loop and the zigzag
sec.t:
The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway opened in 1881. Its rails are just 610 mm apart, less than the width of a school desk. It climbs from the plains near Siliguri to about 2,258 m at Ghum, one of the highest stations in India, before dropping slightly to Darjeeling.

To gain height, engineers used two tricks. At loops such as the Batasia Loop, the train spirals around and passes over its own track. At zigzags, it drives forward up one slope, stops, then reverses up the next. Little blue steam engines first built in the 1880s and 1890s still puff along parts of the route.

In the 1969 film Aradhana, Rajesh Khanna sang Mere Sapno Ki Rani from a jeep racing beside this very train.

{{story:steam-engine}}

The Nilgiri Mountain Railway reached Ooty in 1908. On its steepest stretch, between Kallar and Coonoor, the slope is about 1 in 12. That means climbing 1 m for every 12 m forward, steeper than many roads.

Normal wheels would just spin on such a slope. So this section has a third rail with teeth, laid between the two running rails. A cogwheel under the engine locks into it, like [[@gears|gears]] meshing in a bicycle. The 46 km trip uphill takes around five hours, which makes it one of India's slowest trains.

The Kalka–Shimla Railway opened in 1903 to carry officials to Shimla, the summer capital. In 96 km it passes through 102 tunnels still in use and crosses hundreds of bridges, some built like stacked Roman arches. The longest tunnel, at Barog, is about 1.1 km long.

A local legend says the engineer who first dug the Barog tunnel, Colonel Barog, got his calculations wrong, and the two ends didn't meet. A villager named Bhalku is said to have helped guide the later builders. Historians can't confirm every detail, but the story is told in Himachal to this day.

The British wanted to reach their [[@india-wonder-hill-stations|hill stations]] quickly, and to carry goods down from the hills. The Darjeeling train hauled tea, timber and supplies. Before it opened, the trip up could take days by cart and pony. These lines grew out of the larger [[@indian-railways|Indian railway network]] spreading across the plains.

The USA has climbing trains too. The Mount Washington Cog Railway in New Hampshire, opened in 1868, was the first of its kind in the world. Its engines also grip a toothed rail.

The toy trains still run, though landslides and [[monsoon|monsoon]] damage sometimes close parts of the lines for months. Tourists book months ahead, especially for steam rides. Some trips take longer than driving, but nobody rides a toy train to save time. On the Darjeeling line the track runs right through town markets, so shopkeepers step back from their stalls as the engine squeezes past.

They earned UNESCO status in stages: Darjeeling in 1999, Nilgiri in 2005 and Kalka–Shimla in 2008. What decides whether a place joins that list is explained in [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Sites]].

text: Yosemite (say yoh-SEM-it-ee) is a national park in the mountains of California. Its heart is Yosemite Valley, a deep, flat-floored valley about 11 km long, walled in by grey [[granite|granite]] cliffs and waterfalls. Above it are high meadows, lakes, forests and peaks.

The park covers about 3,000 square kilometres, roughly twice the size of Delhi. Most of the roughly 4 million visitors a year crowd into the valley, which is only a small slice of it. Black bears, mule deer and peregrine falcons live there, and in the south of the park stand groves of giant sequoias, some of the biggest trees on Earth.
The bears are clever at breaking into cars that smell of food, so visitors must lock snacks and cool boxes in metal bear-proof lockers. In 1984 UNESCO named Yosemite a World Heritage Site.

st.prompt: Yosemite Valley is shaped like a giant U. What mostly carved it that way?

options.t: Glaciers grinding through the rock during ice ages
A huge earthquake splitting the mountains apart
Wind blowing sand against the cliffs

st.reveal: Rivers first cut a narrow V-shaped canyon. Then glaciers, rivers of slow-moving ice, filled it during ice ages and scraped the sides wide and steep. That turned the V into a U.

src: US National Park Service, Yosemite National Park.

sec.t:
El Capitan is a single block of granite rising about 900 m (3,000 ft) above the valley floor. [[@sport-climbing|Climbers]] from around the world spend days clinging to it, sleeping on ledges or in tents hung from the cliff. In 2017 the American climber Alex Honnold climbed it with no rope at all, in under four hours.

Yosemite Falls drops about 740 m in three steps. In spring, the spray soaks people standing on the bridge below. By September it may be bone dry. In winter, snow closes the high road across the park, and a cone of ice can build up at the foot of the upper fall. Each February, if the sky is clear and the snowmelt is just right, the setting sun lights up thin Horsetail Fall so it glows like [[lava|lava]].

sec.h: The first people of the valley
sec.t:
Long before the park existed, the Ahwahneechee people lived in the valley they called Ahwahnee. They gathered acorns from the oak trees and traded with neighbouring groups across the mountains, much like other [[@native-nations|Native nations]] of the West.

In 1851, during the California Gold Rush, armed men entered the valley and forced most of them out. Some families later came back and worked in the park. Their [[descendant|descendants]] still live in the region, and the park now works with them to tell their history.

Visitors began arriving soon after, and some worried the valley would be fenced off and sold. In 1864, in the middle of the Civil War, President [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] signed a law handing Yosemite Valley and a grove of sequoias to California to protect "for public use". It was one of the first times any government set aside wild land for everyone.

A Scottish-born writer named John Muir spent years walking the mountains and writing about them. His campaigning helped Yosemite become a national park in 1890. Today the biggest problem is crowds. On busy summer days the valley road can fill with cars like a city street, and the park has sometimes asked visitors to book ahead. The sequoias, some of them close relatives of the [[@redwoods|redwoods]] on the coast, have seen more than a thousand summers and do not seem to mind.

text: Hindi grew slowly over more than a thousand years. Its deep roots go back to [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]], through everyday spoken languages called Prakrits and later forms called Apabhramsha. The standard Hindi used today grew from Khari Boli, the speech of the region around Delhi and Meerut.
Over the centuries it picked up words from Persian, Arabic, Turkish, Portuguese and English. It is written in the Devanagari script, the same one used for Sanskrit, Marathi and Nepali.

In the 2011 [[@census|census]], about 53 crore people in India gave Hindi as their mother tongue, and many more speak it as a second language. That makes it one of the most widely spoken languages in the world.

st.prompt: Which language gave Hindi the word chabi, meaning key?
st.reveal: Portuguese traders and settlers arrived in India in the 1500s. Their word chave (key) became chabi, and armário (cupboard) became almari. Persian and English gave Hindi many other words.

sec.t:
Languages change a little with every generation, like a river slowly shifting its course. The Sanskrit of ancient texts gave way, in everyday speech, to simpler Prakrits. These in turn changed into many regional languages across north India: Braj, Awadhi, Bhojpuri, Maithili and others.

Some of the greatest poetry in the Hindi tradition was written in these regional forms. In the 1500s, Tulsidas wrote the *Ramcharitmanas*, a retelling of the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]], in Awadhi. Surdas sang of Krishna in Braj Bhasha. Saint-poets such as [[@mirabai-kabir|Kabir and Mirabai]] used plain, everyday words that farmers, weavers and traders could understand.

sec.h: Hindi and Urdu, a shared root

sec.t:
Hindi is a magpie language, collecting shiny words from everyone who came. From Persian came *darwaza* (door) and *dukaan* (shop), and through Persian came Arabic words such as *kitab* (book). Portuguese traders, who arrived in the 1500s, left *almari* (cupboard), *chabi* (key), *mez* (table) and *balti* (bucket). English has added *school*, *bus*, *doctor* and hundreds more.

The flow goes the other way too. English speakers say *pyjamas*, *shampoo* and *bungalow* without knowing they are using [[@words-borrowed|words from India]]. Many people now mix Hindi and English in a single sentence, a style nicknamed Hinglish, heard everywhere from college canteens to TV adverts.

On 14 September 1949, India's [[@constituent-assembly|Constituent Assembly]] decided that Hindi, written in Devanagari, would be the official language of the central government, with English continuing alongside it for official work. That date is now celebrated as Hindi Diwas.

The choice was hotly debated, especially by people in states where Tamil, Bengali and other languages are spoken. India's [[@constitution|Constitution]] does not name any national language, and today it lists 22 languages in its Eighth Schedule.

Hindi has also travelled abroad. In the 1800s and early 1900s, many Indian workers sailed to distant British colonies, and forms of Hindi are still spoken by their [[descendant|descendants]] in Fiji, Mauritius, Suriname and Trinidad.

text: Kalidasa was a poet and playwright who wrote in [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]], probably about 1,600 years ago. He is the most celebrated writer of classical Sanskrit, the polished form of the language used for literature in ancient India.
He left behind three plays, two long [[epic|epic]] poems and at least one shorter poem. His play Shakuntala and his poem Meghaduta, "The Cloud Messenger", are read in classrooms from Pune to Paris.

st.prompt: In Kalidasa's Meghaduta, a lonely spirit sends a message to his wife far away. What carries it?
st.reveal: An exiled yaksha in central India asks a monsoon cloud to fly north to his wife in the Himalaya. He describes every river, hill and city the cloud will pass, so the poem doubles as a map of ancient India.

n.certNote: Kalidasa's works are well known, but his life is not. Most scholars place him around the 4th or 5th century CE, possibly at the Gupta court, but there is no firm record.

myth: Kalidasa was once a fool who cut off the very branch he was sitting on, and history records this.
That is a popular folk tale, along with the story that the goddess Kali made him wise. Nothing about his early life is recorded. We know him only through his writing.

sec.t:
We know Kalidasa's words far better than his life. His name means "servant of Kali". Many scholars think he lived during the [[@gupta-golden-age|Gupta age]], perhaps at the court of Chandragupta II, because his works describe a rich, settled kingdom much like that one. A popular legend makes him one of the "nine gems" at the court of a king called Vikramaditya.

Ujjain, in [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]], is often linked with him. He describes the city lovingly in his poems, and an annual festival there, the Kalidas Samaroh, celebrates his work with plays and music.

Meghaduta is a poem of about 110 verses. A yaksha, a kind of nature spirit, has been banished for a year to a hill in central India. When the first [[@clouds-types|monsoon clouds]] arrive, he cannot bear being apart from his wife. So he asks a cloud to carry a message north to the Himalaya.

The poem follows the cloud past rivers, forests and cities, with careful details of birds, flowers and rain. Many poets later wrote their own "messenger poems" in imitation.

Kalidasa's two long poems are grand in scale. Kumarasambhava, "The Birth of Kumara", tells how the goddess Parvati wins the heart of Shiva through years of hard penance in the Himalaya. Their son Kumara, also called Kartikeya, is born to defeat a demon.

Raghuvamsha follows the family line of King Raghu over many generations, including Rama, the hero of the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]]. A shorter poem, Ritusamhara, describes India's six [[@seasons-why|seasons]] one by one, from scorching summer to spring. Some scholars doubt it is really his.

In 1789 William Jones, a British judge in Calcutta who studied Sanskrit, published Shakuntala in English. A German version followed in 1791 and amazed readers in Europe, including the poet Goethe. It was one of the first pieces of Indian literature many Europeans had ever read.

In India, Kalidasa's plays are still performed in Sanskrit and in translation, and they shaped later Indian [[@theatre|theatre]]. His comparisons are what readers remember: a king's mind running back to his love like a silk flag fluttering backwards against the wind.

text: Ginger-garlic paste starts thousands of Indian dishes, from chicken curry to chole. It is so common that shops sell it ready-made in jars. Cooks in China, Korea, Thailand and the Caribbean pair the two as well.

The main reason is flavour. Garlic brings a deep, savoury, slightly sulphur smell. Ginger brings a bright, lemony heat. Together they cover each other's weak spots and make food taste fuller. Both also tame strong smells in meat and fish, both keep well for weeks and both are cheap. Once a pairing works for centuries in kitchens, it gets passed down and becomes "how food is made".

st.prompt: Why does a crushed garlic clove smell much stronger than a whole one?

options.t: Crushing starts a chemical reaction that makes the smell
Crushing lets out air trapped inside the clove

st.reveal: Garlic stores a harmless chemical called alliin in one part of its cells and an enzyme in another. Crushing breaks the walls between them, and they quickly make allicin, the sharp-smelling substance that may help protect the plant from animals.

sec.t:
Ginger and garlic both grow underground, but they're not related. Ginger is a [[rhizome|rhizome]], a swollen sideways stem, from a leafy [[tropical|tropical]] plant related to turmeric and cardamom. Nobody has ever found ginger growing wild, away from farms and gardens. It was probably first grown somewhere in tropical South or Southeast Asia, thousands of years ago.

Garlic is a bulb, a cluster of fleshy leaf bases, and a cousin of [[@onions-tears|onions]]. Its wild ancestors came from the mountains of Central Asia. Ancient Egyptians grew it, and bulbs of garlic were found in Tutankhamun's tomb.

Today India grows more ginger than any other country, much of it in Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka and the Northeast. China grows about three-quarters of the world's garlic, far ahead of India in second place.

Garlic plays a clever trick. A whole clove keeps a chemical called alliin in one part of its cells and an [[enzyme|enzyme]] in another. When you crush or chop it, the two mix and make allicin, which smells sharp and stings the tongue. That's probably how the plant defends itself against hungry animals.

Heat changes allicin into gentler, sweeter compounds. That's why raw garlic bites, while slow-cooked garlic tastes mellow and nutty.

Fresh ginger gets its heat from gingerol. When ginger dries or cooks, some gingerol turns into shogaol, which is even more pungent. Dried ginger powder, called *sonth*, is fiercer than the fresh root.

{{story:silk-road}}

Flavour is mostly [[@taste-smell-link|smell]]. Your tongue picks up sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savoury, but your nose does the rest. Ginger and garlic hit your nose with very different scents at once, so a dish smells complex rather than flat.

In Indian kitchens the paste usually goes into hot oil after the onions have browned. Frying for a minute or two cooks out the raw edge. Then come tomatoes and powdered spices such as [[@turmeric|turmeric]]. Skipping that frying step leaves a curry tasting harsh and raw. Many cooks judge the moment by smell alone: the sharp, green scent fades and a sweeter, toasty one takes over. In South India, the paste often joins [[@curry-leaves|curry leaves]] and [[@mustard|mustard]] seeds, while in the north it meets cumin, cardamom and garam masala.

In Chinese cooking, ginger, garlic and spring onion form a classic trio, tossed into a hot wok before everything else. This is one reason [[@chinese-food-india|Indo-Chinese food]] like chilli chicken feels familiar to Indian tastes.

Some traditions leave the pair out. Many Jains avoid garlic, onions, fresh ginger and other roots, because pulling them up harms the whole plant and the tiny creatures in the soil. Some Hindu communities also cook without garlic and onion, especially on fasting days and in temple kitchens.

Ginger has a long place in traditional medicine. Ayurveda calls it *vishwabheshaj*, "the universal medicine", and ginger tea is a common home remedy for an upset stomach. Some studies suggest ginger can ease mild nausea. Bigger claims, about either ginger or garlic curing serious illness, aren't backed by good evidence. If someone is unwell, the best plan is still to see a doctor.
